title: C and How It Builds
summary: C is a small, fast language close to the machine, created in 1972 to write Unix. A C program is text that a compiler turns into machine code in steps - preprocess, compile, assemble, link - and every program starts in a function called main.
markdown:
## Why C C was created by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs in 1972 to write the Unix operating system (the Computer Fundamentals course tells the story in lesson 5.04). Fifty years later it is still everywhere: - operating system kernels: Linux, and the cores of Windows and macOS; - small chips in cars, washing machines, routers and medical devices; - databases (SQLite, PostgreSQL), and the interpreters of other languages: **Python's main interpreter is written in C**. C is small - the whole language fits in a short book - and it is close to the machine: you decide exactly how much memory each value takes and where it lives. That makes it fast and powerful, and also unforgiving: C trusts you, and does not stop you from making a mistake. This course teaches the power and the care together. ## The first program ```c #include int main(void) { printf("Hello, world!\n"); return 0; } ``` Press **Run**. Line by line: | Line | Meaning | |---|---| | `#include ` | Bring in the declarations of the standard input/output functions, such as `printf` | | `int main(void)` | Every C program starts in the function `main`. It takes nothing (`void`) and gives back an `int` | | `{ ... }` | The body of the function | | `printf("Hello, world!\n");` | Print the text. `\n` is a new line. Every statement ends with `;` | | `return 0;` | Finish, telling the operating system "all went well" (0). Any other number means something went wrong | ## How C becomes a program C is a **compiled** language: before it runs, a compiler turns the text into machine code. It happens in four steps: ```mermaid flowchart LR S["hello.c
your source"] -->|1 preprocess| P["#include and
#define done"] P -->|2 compile| A["assembly"] A -->|3 assemble| O["object file
(machine code)"] O -->|4 link| E["hello
(a program)"] L["libraries:
the code of printf"] --> E ``` 1. **Preprocess**: lines starting with `#` are handled first. `#include ` is replaced by the contents of that header file. 2. **Compile**: the C code is translated into assembly for your CPU. 3. **Assemble**: the assembly becomes machine code, in an **object file**. 4. **Link**: your object file is joined with the libraries it uses (the machine code of `printf` lives in the C standard library) into one program. On your own computer you would run one command, which does all four: ```bash gcc hello.c -o hello # or: clang hello.c -o hello ./hello ``` On Windows with Visual Studio the command is `cl hello.c`. On this site, pressing Run does it for you with GCC. ## Compiler errors and warnings When the compiler cannot understand the code, it stops with an **error** and the line number. When the code is valid but suspicious, it gives a **warning** and builds anyway. Treat warnings as errors you have not met yet: most of them point at a real bug. ```c-norun #include int main(void) { printf("Hello, world!\n") // error: expected ';' before 'return' return 0; } ``` The error is reported on the line *after* the missing semicolon, because that is where the compiler noticed. When an error makes no sense, look at the line above. ## Comments ```c #include /* A comment can span several lines like this. */ int main(void) { // and this kind runs to the end of the line printf("Comments are ignored by the compiler.\n"); return 0; } ``` ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Where does every C program start running? - At the first line of the file + In the function main - In stdio.h > The operating system calls main. ? What does #include do? - It downloads the library from the internet + It inserts the declarations of functions like printf - It marks the line where the program starts > Before compiling, the preprocessor replaces the line with the header's contents: the declarations of the standard input/output functions. ? What does return 0; at the end of main tell the operating system? - The program printed nothing - To run the program again + The program finished successfully > 0 means success; other values mean an error. ? Which step joins your code with the code of printf? - Preprocessing - Assembling + Linking > printf's machine code lives in the C standard library; the linker joins them. ```

cards.q: Where does every C program start running?
cards.a:
In the function main

The operating system calls main.

It inserts the declarations of functions like printf

Before compiling, the preprocessor replaces the line with the header's contents: the declarations of the standard input/output functions.

cards.q: What does return 0; at the end of main tell the operating system?
cards.a:
The program finished successfully

0 means success; other values mean an error.

cards.q: Which step joins your code with the code of printf?
cards.a:
Linking

printf's machine code lives in the C standard library; the linker joins them.
